curiosities.label: Angles grouped
curiosities.plain: How the shots of a scene are planned as a set. momentum.plot: A shift in the shadows' color can tell the audience the story has turned before anyone says so.
momentum.theme: Cool shadows and warm faces is the look of a film about people warmer than their world.
momentum.pull: Color the eye didn't expect pulls it to the part of the frame that changed.
momentum.tryThis: Turn the shadows cold the moment the secret comes out.

curiosities.label: Color curves
curiosities.plain: Bending the brightness, or one color channel (only the red, the green or the blue in the picture), with a curve: Final Cut's color curves and hue and saturation curves.

sliders.label: Curve shape
sliders.plain: Flat (no change), gentle S or strong S (an S-shaped curve: darks darker and brights brighter, so more contrast), faded blacks (the darkest parts lifted to a soft gray), crushed blacks (dark detail pushed to solid black) or inverted (like a negative).

sliders.label: Channel
sliders.plain: Which part of the color the curve bends: all of it, only the red, green or blue channel (one of the three colors every picture is mixed from), or how strong each hue is (hue vs saturation).

sliders.label: Amount
sliders.plain: How far the curve bends.

momentum.plot: A strong curve hardens a scene as it gets serious.
momentum.theme: Faded blacks read as memory or nostalgia.
momentum.pull: Contrast pulls the eye to the brightest face.
momentum.tryThis: Fade the blacks for the flashback, then crush them when you come back.

curiosities.label: Animation feel
curiosities.plain: How the movement itself feels: stiff or rubbery, snappy or smooth, real or cartoon. The twelve old rules of animation, as sliders.

sliders.label: Kind of movement
sliders.plain: From movement that looks like a machine, through real life, to cartoon bodies that bend like rubber hoses.

sliders.label: Slow into and out of poses
sliders.plain: Whether moves start and stop gently (ease in and out) or at full speed. In Maya this is the shape of the curve between keys.

sliders.label: Wind-up before a move
sliders.plain: The small move the other way before the big one: crouch before a jump, pull back before a punch.

sliders.label: Overshoot and settle
sliders.plain: Going a little past the end pose and settling back, like a hand that stops and wobbles.

sliders.label: Parts that keep moving
sliders.plain: Hair, ears, coats and bellies that keep going after the body stops (follow-through and overlapping action).

sliders.label: Curved paths
sliders.plain: Whether hands and heads travel in curves (alive) or straight lines (mechanical).

sliders.label: Squash and stretch
sliders.plain: How much bodies squash on impact and stretch in speed. Zero is solid; five is a bouncing ball.

sliders.label: Exaggeration
sliders.plain: How far poses and timing are pushed past real life to make a point read.

sliders.label: Stillness
sliders.plain: How long a character stays in a pose before the next move. Long freezes are a comedy tool.

sliders.label: Little extra actions
sliders.plain: Small actions on top of the main one: tapping a foot while waiting, fiddling with a pen while talking.

sliders.label: Poses per beat
sliders.plain: How many clear poses a move goes through. More poses read as busier, fewer as bolder.

momentum.plot: How a character moves tells the audience what they want before they say it: a rushed, stiff walk is heading somewhere it dreads.
momentum.theme: Stiff against loose movement is a theme of control against freedom.
momentum.pull: A change in how someone moves (the stiff one suddenly loose) is a change the eye catches at once.
momentum.tryThis: Animate the uptight character stiffly, then give them one cartoony move the moment they let go.

curiosities.label: Time and speed
curiosities.plain: How time runs in the shot: real time, slow motion, sped up, frozen, played backwards, smooth or choppy like stop-motion.

sliders.label: Speed of time
sliders.plain: How fast time runs in this moment, from stopped to racing.

sliders.label: Speed change
sliders.plain: Whether the speed changes inside the shot, like an action shot that slows down for the hit and speeds up again.

sliders.label: Smooth or choppy
sliders.plain: Drawn on ones is smooth; twos is snappy (classic hand-drawn); threes is choppy, like stop-motion.

sliders.label: Forward or back
sliders.plain: Whether time plays forward, stops, or runs backwards for a moment.

sliders.label: Repeats
sliders.plain: Whether a bit of action plays again: a replay for a joke, or a loop that traps a character.

momentum.plot: Slowing or freezing time tells the audience: this moment decides everything that follows.
momentum.theme: Stretched time shows a moment someone will remember forever; sped-up time shows a stretch that does not matter.
momentum.pull: When time slows, the audience leans in and waits for the thing that is about to happen.
momentum.tryThis: Freeze the frame on the worst possible moment, then hold it one beat longer than is comfortable.

curiosities.label: Poses and body control
curiosities.plain: How strong and clear a pose is: the line through the body, the outline, balance, where the feet are planted, what the hands hold.

sliders.label: Line through the body
sliders.plain: Imagine one line from head to foot. A strong curve reads as energy and intent; straight reads as stiff or formal.

sliders.label: Clear outline
sliders.plain: Whether you could tell what the character is doing from a black shadow of them alone.

sliders.label: Balance
sliders.plain: Where the weight sits: tipping over, moving from foot to foot, or rooted to the spot.

sliders.label: Feet on the ground
sliders.plain: Whether the feet stay fixed where they land (what IK is for in Maya) or leave the ground.

sliders.label: Twist in the body
sliders.plain: How much the shoulders turn against the hips. Twist makes a pose look alive.

sliders.label: What the hands hold
sliders.plain: Whether the hands are free or locked to something (a constraint in Maya).

sliders.label: Even or uneven
sliders.plain: Both sides of the body doing the same thing looks stiff; uneven poses look natural.

momentum.plot: A strong pose shows what a character is about to do, so the audience is a step ahead of the plot.
momentum.theme: How someone holds their body says how they feel about their place in the world.
momentum.pull: The eye reads a clear outline before a word is said, so a strong pose grabs attention first.
momentum.tryThis: Hold the strongest pose of the scene for the line that turns it.

curiosities.label: Face acting
curiosities.plain: What the face does: how big the expression is, brows, eyes, mouth, blinks, which side moves, and how fast it changes.

sliders.label: Size of the expression
sliders.plain: How much the face shows, from a poker face to a cartoon take.

sliders.label: Eyebrows
sliders.plain: Brows down read as anger or focus; up reads as surprise, worry or hope.

sliders.label: Eyes
sliders.plain: How open the eyes are.

sliders.label: Mouth
sliders.plain: The shape of the mouth, from holding it in to letting it all out.

sliders.label: Eyes darting
sliders.plain: Quick small eye movements: a thinking, nervous or lying face darts; a calm or certain face holds still.

sliders.label: Blinks
sliders.plain: Blinks per beat. A blink often marks a new thought.

sliders.label: One side or both
sliders.plain: Whether both sides of the face move the same. A one-sided smile is a smirk or a sneer.

sliders.label: Lip sync
sliders.plain: How closely the mouth matches the words.

sliders.label: How fast it changes
sliders.plain: Whether a feeling spreads across the face slowly or snaps on.

sliders.label: Pushes the story
sliders.plain: How much this curiosity moves the story forward here.

momentum.plot: A face changing tells the audience a decision has been made before the character acts on it.
momentum.theme: What the face hides against what it shows is where the theme of honesty lives.
momentum.pull: Close on a face, the audience watches for the smallest change and reads it as the next turn.
momentum.tryThis: Let the face change a beat before the line, so the audience knows what is coming and dreads it.

sliders.label: How alike
sliders.plain: Whether they look like copies (funny or creepy) or each one is their own person.

sliders.label: In step
sliders.plain: Whether they move separately or as one, like a marching band.

sliders.label: How they are spread
sliders.plain: How the crowd is laid out in the space.

sliders.label: Follow the leader
sliders.plain: Whether the crowd copies one person.

sliders.label: Ripple delay
sliders.plain: How long it takes a move to pass through the crowd, like a stadium wave.

momentum.theme: A crowd moving as one is the theme of the herd against the person.
momentum.pull: One figure out of step in a perfect crowd is where the eye goes.
momentum.tryThis: Put one person out of step in a perfect crowd, and make that person matter later.

curiosities.label: Light setup
curiosities.plain: What kind of lights light the scene and how they work together: the sun, the sky, a window, a spotlight, a bare bulb; how bright the dark side is; light bouncing off walls. Close to "Lighting"; this one is about the kinds of lights and how they work together, that one gathers direction, hardness, warmth and shape.

sliders.label: Main light
sliders.plain: The kind of light doing most of the work.

sliders.label: Bright side to dark side
sliders.plain: How much darker the shadow side of a face is than the lit side.

sliders.label: Light bouncing around
sliders.plain: Light bouncing off walls and floors and filling the room with soft color (global illumination).

sliders.label: How far the light reaches
sliders.plain: Whether the light fills the whole space or falls into darkness a few steps away.

sliders.label: Who the light touches
sliders.plain: Lights that touch only some things, a trick for making one person glow.

sliders.label: Hard or soft
sliders.plain: Hard light makes sharp shadows; soft light wraps around faces.

sliders.label: Rim light
sliders.plain: A light from behind that draws a bright edge around a person.

sliders.label: Haze and beams
sliders.plain: Haze in the air that makes beams of light visible.

sliders.label: Shaped light
sliders.plain: Light cut into shapes: blinds, leaves, a window frame.

sliders.label: Lamps in the shot
sliders.plain: Whether the lights themselves (lamps, candles, screens) are visible in the picture.

momentum.plot: A change in the lights (a door opening, a lamp going out) marks a turn without a word.
momentum.theme: Light against dark is the oldest picture of hope against fear.
momentum.pull: The eye goes to the brightest thing in the frame, so light steers attention.
momentum.tryThis: Light only the person who is lying, and let everyone else fall into shadow.

curiosities.label: Surfaces and materials
curiosities.plain: What things are made of, as the light shows it: matte or shiny, metal or glass, smooth or bumpy, worn or new.

sliders.label: Kind of surface
sliders.plain: What the surface looks like it is made of, by how it takes the light.

sliders.label: Shine
sliders.plain: How much the surface reflects, from chalk to a polished car.

sliders.label: See-through
sliders.plain: Whether light passes through: a wall, frosted glass, a clean window.

sliders.label: Texture
sliders.plain: How bumpy the surface looks up close.

sliders.label: Clear coat
sliders.plain: A shiny layer on top, like varnish on wood or the paint on a car.

sliders.label: Soft fuzz
sliders.plain: The soft glow at the edges of fabrics like velvet and peach skin.

sliders.label: Rainbow film
sliders.plain: Rainbow colors on a surface, like oil on a puddle.

sliders.label: Wet
sliders.plain: How wet surfaces look, from dry to dripping.

sliders.label: Glows
sliders.plain: Whether the surface gives off its own light.

sliders.label: Wear
sliders.plain: Scratches, dust and rust: how much life the surface has seen.

momentum.theme: What things are made of says what a world values: marble and gold, or plywood and tape.

curiosities.label: Skin
curiosities.plain: How skin looks in the light: plastic or alive, dry or sweaty, pale or flushed, airbrushed or every pore.

sliders.label: Light through the skin
sliders.plain: Real skin lets light in and glows a little, like ears lit from behind (subsurface scattering).

sliders.label: Skin in the light
sliders.plain: How the light sits on the skin.

sliders.label: Dry to sweaty
sliders.plain: How much shine sweat and oil put on the face. Sweat is a tension tool.

sliders.label: Color in the face
sliders.plain: Blood in the face: fear drains it; anger, shame and love bring it.

sliders.label: Detail
sliders.plain: How smooth or real the skin looks up close.

momentum.plot: A face going pale or red shows a feeling the character is trying to hide, before they act on it.
momentum.theme: Airbrushed against real skin is a theme of the polished image against the true person.
momentum.pull: Sweat on a forehead makes the audience feel the pressure and wait for the crack.
momentum.tryThis: Add a bead of sweat in the close-up just before the lie.

curiosities.label: Drawn or real look
curiosities.plain: Whether the picture looks like a photo, a painting, a cartoon or a comic: outlines, flat color bands, hatching and paper.

sliders.label: Look
sliders.plain: Photo-real, painted, cartoon or flat graphic.

sliders.label: Outline weight
sliders.plain: How thick the drawn lines around things are.

sliders.label: Shading
sliders.plain: Smooth shading looks rounded and real; two flat bands look like a cartoon (cel shading).

sliders.label: Hatching
sliders.plain: Shadows drawn with lines, like an ink comic or an old engraving.

sliders.label: Line wobble
sliders.plain: Lines that shake a little from drawing to drawing look hand-made and alive.

sliders.label: Paper
sliders.plain: The texture of paper under the picture.

momentum.plot: Switching the look (photo to cartoon) can mark a dream, a memory or a story inside the story.
momentum.theme: A drawn look says the film is a told story; a real look says it is happening.
momentum.pull: A sudden change of look makes the audience ask why, and watch for the answer.
momentum.tryThis: Switch to a sketchy, hand-drawn look when the character starts to imagine.

curiosities.label: Layers of the picture
curiosities.plain: The picture as layers you can turn up and down: foreground against background, contact shadows (the dark where things touch), fog that grows with distance, and one light group (a set of lights mixed together as one) louder than another.

sliders.label: Foreground against background
sliders.plain: How clearly the picture splits into near, middle and far.

sliders.label: Fog with distance
sliders.plain: Things far away fade into haze, which makes space feel deep.

sliders.label: Contact shadows
sliders.plain: The dark where things touch (a cup on a table, feet on a floor) that makes them sit in the world (ambient occlusion).

sliders.label: Light mix
sliders.plain: Which group of lights (a set of lights mixed together as one) is turned up when the layers are combined.

sliders.label: One thing on its own
sliders.plain: Pulling one object out on its own layer, to brighten, blur or color it alone.

momentum.plot: Pulling one thing forward from the background tells the audience it will matter.
momentum.theme: Deep layered space feels like a full world; one flat layer feels like a stage or a memory.
momentum.pull: The layer that is brightest and sharpest is the one the eye goes to.
momentum.tryThis: Fade the background into fog as the character shuts the world out.

curiosities.label: The camera lens
curiosities.plain: The glass in front of the camera: wide or long, how much is in focus, focus moving from one thing to another, motion blur, shake, bending at the edges, flares.

sliders.label: Wide or long
sliders.plain: A wide lens shows a lot and stretches space; a long lens shows a little and squashes it flat.

sliders.label: How much is sharp
sliders.plain: Everything sharp, or just one thing sharp with the rest soft.

sliders.label: Focus moves
sliders.plain: Focus moving from one thing to another during the shot.

sliders.label: Motion blur
sliders.plain: How much fast things smear.

sliders.label: Shake
sliders.plain: How much the camera shakes. Shot that way: same as "Camera shake while filming". "Camera move added in the edit" adds a shake in the edit, and "Shake removed in the edit" removes it.

sliders.label: Bending at the edges
sliders.plain: How much the lens bends straight lines at the edges of the picture.

sliders.label: Flares
sliders.plain: Light catching in the lens: a glint or long streaks.

sliders.label: Dark corners
sliders.plain: Darkening at the corners that pulls the eye to the middle.

sliders.label: Pushes the story

curiosities.plain: The weather turns with the feeling: a storm breaks during the fight, the sun comes out when they make up, rain falls at the funeral. Writers call it pathetic fallacy. Close to "Making something tiny epic", which blows small things up into grand ones; this one borrows the tools of one exact kind of film (a genre).

curiosities.label: Every problem in one room
curiosities.plain: All the lies, secrets and running problems of the story end up in the same room at the same time: the wife, the lover, the boss and the police all arrive for dinner. Close to "Chaos in an orderly room", which measures the disorder; this one is every story thread meeting at once, the big finish of a farce (a comedy of lies, doors and bad timing).

sliders.plain: Who is running around keeping the wrong people apart.

curiosities.label: Copying someone, badly
curiosities.plain: One character copies another to fit in or to impress: the same walk, the same order at the cafe, the same laugh, but always a little wrong or a beat late. Close to "Copying each other's body", which is two people falling into the same moves without thinking; this one is copying on purpose, and getting it wrong.

curiosities.label: Keeping the eye in place across the cut
curiosities.plain: When one shot ends, the audience is looking at one spot. If the next shot puts the important thing in that same spot, the eye never has to search and a fast run of shots feels smooth. If the next shot puts it somewhere else, the eye has to jump, which can feel like a jolt. Editors call this eye trace.

sliders.label: How well the spot matches
sliders.plain: From the eye has to hunt all over the new shot (0) to the subject is exactly where the eye already was (5).

sliders.label: Where the eye sits at the cut

sliders.plain: What guides the eye to that spot just before the cut.

curiosities.label: Everyone looks the same way
curiosities.plain: A whole room, or a whole crowd, turns to look at the same thing: a door that opens, a sound, one person standing up. The audience's eyes follow theirs, and we badly want to see what they see. Filmmakers use it to announce that something new has arrived.

sliders.label: How much of the frame turns
sliders.plain: From one or two heads turning (0) to every single person in the frame turning at once (5).

sliders.plain: What pulls all the eyes.

sliders.plain: How long the film makes us wait before showing what they are looking at.

momentum.tryThis: In the busy diner, let every head turn to the door at once, and hold on their faces before we see who walked in.

curiosities.label: Something that doesn't belong
curiosities.plain: A small thing in the frame that is wrong: a wet footprint on a dry floor, a clock showing the wrong time, a bandage nobody mentions, a stranger standing in the back. The audience notices it and starts to wonder, which keeps them watching closely.

sliders.label: How strange it is
sliders.plain: From barely odd (0) to clearly impossible (5).

sliders.plain: The kind of detail that does not belong.

curiosities.label: How far apart the surprises come
curiosities.plain: The rhythm of surprise across the film: how many there are, how far apart, and whether they grow. Surprises too close together wear the audience out; too far apart and they drift. Many films space them so the gaps get shorter toward the end.

sliders.label: How surprising the story is
sliders.plain: From you can see everything coming (0) to a surprise around every corner (5).

curiosities.label: The promise of the opening
curiosities.plain: The first minutes of a film tell the audience what kind of ride this will be: laughs, fear, a mystery, a love story. That promise is why people keep watching. A film that keeps its promise, and then gives more than it promised, feels like it is going somewhere.

sliders.label: How clear the promise is
sliders.plain: From the opening could lead anywhere (0) to we know exactly what kind of film this is (5).

sliders.plain: The kind of film the opening says this is.

curiosities.label: A stretch where nothing pulls
curiosities.plain: A part of the film where nothing is pulling the audience forward: no question open, no goal in sight, no clock. Attention drifts and people reach for their phones. Sometimes a rest is planned; often it is an accident that needs a fix.

sliders.label: How flat the stretch feels
sliders.plain: From still pulling us along (0) to attention drifting right away (5).

curiosities.label: Leaving at the best part
curiosities.plain: When a film follows two or more stories, it can leave one at its most exciting moment and cut to the other: the hero is hanging from the ledge, and we go to a calm kitchen across town. The audience is pulled through the other story to get back. Old writers called it streaky bacon: layers of fat and lean.

sliders.label: How close to the peak we leave
sliders.plain: From leaving once the trouble is over (0) to leaving one second before the answer (5).

sliders.label: Stories we cut between
sliders.plain: How many different stories the film keeps going at once.

sliders.plain: At what point in the moment we cut away.

sliders.plain: How long until we come back to the story we left.

curiosities.label: The answer almost given
curiosities.plain: A character is about to say the thing we most want to know (who did it, where it is hidden, how they really feel) and something stops them. The answer slips away, and we want it twice as much.

curiosities.label: The closed box we want opened
curiosities.plain: A thing the audience can see but not see inside: a locked briefcase, a sealed letter, a door no one opens, a phone with one unread message. It sits in the story asking a question all by itself.

curiosities.label: One answer opens a bigger question
curiosities.plain: Each time the film answers a question, the answer brings a new and bigger one: we learn who sent the letter, and now we must know why. The audience never runs out of questions, so the story feels like it keeps going deeper.

curiosities.label: The clue that points the wrong way
curiosities.plain: A clue that leads the audience, and often the hero, to the wrong answer: the suspicious neighbor who turns out to be innocent, the weapon that was never used. Mystery writers call it a red herring. A good one is fair: it makes sense once the truth comes out.

curiosities.label: Knowing what they want in this scene
curiosities.plain: In every scene, someone wants something: to get the keys, to leave, to hear the truth. When the audience knows what that is, they can root for it and feel each step closer or further. When nobody knows, the scene drifts, however pretty it looks.

curiosities.label: A rule we learn early
curiosities.plain: Early on, the film tells us a rule of its world: never feed them after midnight, the door only opens once, if you say the name it comes. From then on the audience watches for that rule to be broken, and every near miss feels dangerous.

curiosities.label: Asking our question for us
curiosities.plain: A character says out loud exactly what the audience is wondering: "Wait, why did he lie?" It tells us the film knows, that we are not confused but curious, and it sharpens the question so we carry it forward.

curiosities.label: Time to take in the shot

In the spirit of Monty Python.

suites.label: Fast visual comedy cut to the beat
suites.plain: Jokes told by the edit: quick close shots of everyday actions, whip pans between places, a whoosh or a thud on every move, cuts that land on the music, shapes that match from one shot to the next, and small details planted early that pay off later. In the spirit of Edgar Wright. A whip pan is a camera turn so fast that the picture blurs into the next shot.

scenes.title: Model scene: A sandwich at 3 a.m., cut to the beat
scenes.plain: Practice for the style "Fast visual comedy cut to the beat": a night-shift nurse comes home at 3 a.m. and builds the perfect sandwich. scenes.title: Model scene: A balloon seller loses every balloon
scenes.plain: Practice for the style "Sweet clown with a broken heart": a balloon seller in a frayed old tailcoat loses every balloon he owns, one mishap at a time, on the day he means to give one to the florist across the square. He never says a word, he keeps falling down, and the laughs turn slowly into tears.

beats.note: a man in a frayed tailcoat with a fistful of red balloons; across the square, a florist opens her shop
he crosses to her; he bows each time she offers a hand, three times over, and they bump heads

scenes.title: Model scene: A manager throws his own birthday party
scenes.plain: Practice for the style "Squirm comedy of the clueless boss": the manager of a small paper warehouse throws himself a surprise birthday party on the day his own boss visits from head office. He tries far too hard to be cool, his jokes land on nothing, he explains each one, and the silences go on and on while his staff glance at the camera.

beats.note: a break room, a cake he bought for himself; he greets the woman from head office with a fist and slang ten years old

scenes.title: Model scene: A polite war of compliments at a garden wedding
scenes.plain: Practice for the style "Romantic comedy of manners": at a grand garden wedding, a hired portrait painter and the bride's widowed aunt, who are secretly in love, fight a perfectly polite war of compliments. Everything that matters happens behind a closed door or in a dropped note, every kind word means its opposite, and we always know more than the guests do.

beats.note: a lawn, a string quartet, a long table of cakes no one is allowed to touch yet
'What a bold hat.' 'What a truthful portrait.' Each smiles, and each means it as a wound

scenes.title: Model scene: A rider walks across town for her bike
scenes.plain: Practice for the style "Handheld realism": a young food delivery rider finds her bike gone from outside a block of flats and walks across the cold town to the council pound to get it back before her shift. scenes.plain: Practice for the style "Horror jump scare build": a babysitter goes down to the basement laundry room at night because the dryer has stopped mid-cycle. scenes.title: Model scene: The electric meter runs out
scenes.plain: Practice for the style "Kitchen-sink realism": on a rainy weeknight in a small rented flat, a warehouse worker who has just been suspended over a missed shift tells her teenage son, while the prepaid electric meter runs out. scenes.title: Model scene: The last crossing of the ferry cafe
scenes.plain: Practice for the style "Deadpan stillness and long pauses": on a small night ferry, the cook in the onboard cafe and the one lorry driver who eats there every night sit through the cafe's very last crossing before it closes for good. Nobody moves, nobody shows a thing, an old song plays on the jukebox, a crash in the kitchen gets no reaction at all, and a sad fact said flatly is the funniest line in the scene.

'Where were you on the night of the fourth?' 'In the garden.' 'Which garden?' 'This one.' 'Let the record show.' The boy writes down 'the record show'
a witness goes to the shed for the evidence; we hear ladders, pots, a bike and a lawnmower fall one by one; he walks back calmly holding a single leaf

beats.note: the two men meet across the hedge, one on an upturned bucket; 'You cut my side!' Thunder cracks on the word 'side', and the shadow of a hedge trimmer towers up the fence

beats.note: the judge rules 'cut it down the middle', and they saw the whole hedge in half lengthways; the postman hands over a letter: the hedge is protected

scenes.title: Model scene: One night to get a concert wristband back
scenes.plain: Practice for the style "One wild night teen comedy": a careful girl and her wild best friend have one night, before concert doors close at eleven, to get back the wristband she left in her dad's car. Her nine-step plan fails at step one, a bowling alley turns into the most public embarrassment of her life, they run the whole way and miss the doors anyway, and at dawn on a car park roof they finally say what the night was really about.

beats.note: in her bedroom, the careful one has a nine-step plan on a whiteboard; the wild one is already halfway out of the window
step one: the garage is locked and the car is not in it; on her phone, a little car icon sits at the bowling alley across town
in the wild one's huge leather jacket, she sneaks past her dad's lane, slips, and slides the whole length of lane six on her back; the big screen shows a strike
she walks back up the lane, car keys in her fist, past every table; one small boy claps slowly; by the door it is already online as a 'bowling stunt'
her dad spots them; they sprint through a car wash and a fish shop and reach the venue at 11:02 as the doors swing shut; the music stops dead
dawn on a car park roof: the wristband was in the jacket pocket all along, snapped in half; she admits she only wanted the concert because the wild one moves away on Monday
they each tie half the wristband on, lean on the rail the same way, notice, and laugh; the sun comes up over the town

scenes.title: Model scene: Two boys chase the class parrot through a party
scenes.plain: Practice for the style "One wild night teen comedy": the class parrot two boys were meant to mind for the weekend has flown off inside a box of decorations to the biggest house party in town, and their teacher collects it at eight in the morning. The careful one is dragged inside by the wild one, who is taken for the booked DJ; there is a fumbled hello with a classmate, karaoke in front of everyone, a chase, and a dawn at the school gate.

beats.note: outside a big house thumping with music: the careful one holds an empty bird cage; the wild one fixes his hair in a car window
the wild one strides in with the cage like a trophy; the host cries 'the DJ is here!' and he does not correct her
the careful one runs into the girl from chemistry class; his high five meets her hug three times until their heads knock
the host stands on a chair to make a toast; from the chandelier, the parrot cuts in with the teacher's exact voice: 'Phones away, please'

beats.note: the only thing the parrot comes down for is the class song, so he sings it alone on the karaoke machine; he glances up and sees the girl from chemistry filming, smiling

values.sceneStealer.when: in the middle of a speech

beats.note: the real DJ arrives; they run, cage in arms, through the pool and over a hedge, stop in a quiet street, catch their breath, and look down: the cage is empty

values.sceneStealer.when: in the middle of a speech

beats.note: at the school gate at dawn, the careful one thanks the wild one for dragging him along; the parrot flies down into the cage and says, in his voice, the first line of the song

scenes.title: Model scene: The torn page in the lighthouse logbook
scenes.plain: Practice for steering attention in a mystery: a young inspector arrives at a lighthouse the morning after the keeper went missing. A clock that stopped at the wrong time catches our eye, a wet coat points at the wrong man, the locked logbook with one page torn out pulls at us the whole scene, and just as the keeper's sister starts to say what happened that night, the foghorn drowns her out.

beats.note: the lighthouse in grey rain at dawn; the inspector climbs the iron stairs behind the keeper's sister
the keeper's room is neat as a pin, but the clock on the wall has stopped at ten past four, and nobody looks at it

values.oddDetail.kind: a wrong time on a clock

beats.note: the logbook sits in a locked tin on the desk; through the glass lid we can see one page has been torn out

values.oddDetail.kind: a wrong time on a clock

beats.note: the sister points out the window at the fisherman's wet coat on the rail: he was here last night, she says, and her hands won't keep still

values.oddDetail.kind: a wrong time on a clock

beats.note: she sits, takes a breath, and starts: 'The light went out at four, and he went down to...' and the door bangs open: the fisherman, dripping

scenes.title: Model scene: The sealed case on the night train
scenes.plain: Practice for steering attention in a thriller: a courier must carry a sealed case from one end of a night train to the other before the border stop, and she has been told one rule: never let it touch the floor. Each shot hands our eye to the next so the walk feels like one long push, the film leaves her at the worst moment to check on the guard working down the train, and the shots get so short we barely read them.

beats.note: a man in the first carriage hands her the case: 'Front to back before the border. It never touches the floor.'
she walks the corridors, the case always on the right of the frame; every cut finds it in the same place, so the walk never stops
the train lurches; the case slips from her fingers toward the floor... and we cut to the border guard, stamping papers one carriage away
back to her: she caught it an inch from the floor; a flash of the label on the case, gone before we can read it
the guard's hand lands on her shoulder: the cut throws his face into the far corner of the frame and our eye has to jump to find it
'Ticket.' She hands it over with her free hand; the case hangs in the other. The music stops dead. Cut to black.

scenes.title: Model scene: The recipe tin at the kitchen table
scenes.plain: Practice for steering attention in a family drama: after their mother's funeral, three grown siblings sit around her kitchen table with her old recipe tin. The youngest grandchild says out loud the question nobody will ask, the whole table turns to look at the eldest, and she almost tells them why she stopped coming home before the kettle whistles and she changes her mind.

beats.note: a small kitchen after the funeral; the brother sorts cards from the recipe tin, the eldest sister stands by the window, a child colors at the end of the table
the child, not looking up from her drawing: 'Why didn't Auntie ever come for Christmas?' Nobody answers.
one by one the brother and the other sister turn to look at the eldest by the window; she keeps looking out at the garden
'Because Mum and I...' The kettle starts to whistle. She stops, takes it off the heat, and says 'It doesn't matter now.'
her brother lifts the last recipe card and finds an envelope underneath, with her name on it in their mother's hand
he slides it across the table; she puts it in her pocket without opening it, and fills the teapot

scenes.title: Model scene: The best man's shuffled speech cards
scenes.plain: Practice for steering attention in a comedy: a nervous best man drops his speech cards on the way to the microphone and reads them in the wrong order. The surprises come closer and closer together, each worse than the last, the whole room turns at once each time a card goes wrong, and a small flower girl keeps asking out loud what everyone is thinking.

beats.note: a wedding hall; the band stops, and the best man walks to the microphone, cards in hand, and trips on a cable; the cards go everywhere
first card: '...and that's why she said no the first time.' Second card: 'Thank you all for coming to the funeral.' He keeps going.
third card: 'Ask her about Paris.' Fifty heads snap round to the bride; only Grandad keeps eating his cake
the flower girl, loud in the silence: 'What happened in Paris?' She asks again after the next card, and the next
he finds the last card, the real one, and reads it plainly: the day he met his friend. The room goes soft for ten seconds
applause; he turns the card over. On the back, in big letters: 'DON'T MENTION PARIS.' Smash to the bride's face

scenes.title: Model scene: The last free throw in the school gym
scenes.plain: Practice for steering attention in a sports moment: a school basketball final is tied with no time left, and the quietest player on the team has two free throws. The whole film has been waiting for her to take a shot like this, the gym turns to watch her in one snap, the clock reads zero, and the ball's flight is slowed down long enough for us to take in every face.

beats.note: the last seconds of a tied final; the gym is roaring; the ball goes up, a whistle: foul on the number 7
the clock reads 0.0; every head in the gym snaps to the number 7, the girl who has passed the ball away all season
the crowd goes soft and blurred; only her face is sharp; we hear her breathing and the ball bounce, three times
she shoots; slowed down, the camera rises over the court and holds long enough to find her mum, her coach, the rival bench, as the ball turns in the air
it drops through clean; the team buries her in a hug; cut as the first teammate lifts her off the floor

scenes.title: Model scene: Two people close the bookshop for the last time
scenes.plain: Practice for steering attention in a romance: two coworkers who have circled each other for years work the last shift before their small bookshop closes for good. A slow middle stretch where they just pack boxes is kept on purpose as a rest, every question one of them answers opens a bigger one, and the kiss the whole film has been holding back finally comes, then gets turned on its head.

beats.note: the shop at dusk, half its shelves empty; an old record on the counter player; they tape boxes and do not look at each other
a quiet stretch: books into boxes, the tape gun, the record crackling; nothing happens and we are let to rest in it
'Are you taking the job in the city?' 'Yes.' 'Why?' 'Because there was no reason to stay.' 'Was there ever?'
she finds a book behind the till with a bus ticket in it, marked at the page they argued about on her first day
they kiss at last, and it is she who pulls back first: 'I'm still going.'
he holds out the shop key; she takes it, locks the door with both of them on the outside, and keeps it

scenes.title: Model scene: The treehouse map with one rule
scenes.plain: Practice for steering attention in a kids' adventure: three friends find a map in their new treehouse, signed by a kid who lived there long ago, with one rule written across the top: never follow it after the streetlights come on. The opening promises a treasure hunt, each clue they solve opens a bigger question, and the rule they learned at the start is broken on purpose at the end.

beats.note: the camera rises up a huge oak to a crooked treehouse; a gust lifts a floorboard and a rolled up map falls at their feet
the map, held up to the light long enough for us to read the rule along the top: NEVER FOLLOW AFTER THE STREETLIGHTS COME ON
the first X is a garden gnome; under it, a key; the key opens the old shed; in the shed, a second map, drawn in the same hand but dated last week
they reach the last X at the end of the lane as the sky goes orange; in the corner of each shot, the streetlight at the end of the road
the streetlight flickers on. They look at each other. The youngest says 'We're so close' and takes the first step
every streetlight down the lane comes on at once, and the hedges part to show a path that was not there in the day

scenes.title: Model scene: The beekeeper on the morning of the first frost
scenes.plain: Practice for steering attention in a quiet documentary-style scene: an old beekeeper checks her hives on the first frosty morning of the year, talking now and then to the camera. The opening tells us plainly this will be slow and calm, long still shots give us time to read every corner, the eye is passed gently from hive to hive across the cuts, and the few small surprises are spaced far apart.

beats.note: frost on a field at dawn; her voice over: 'This might be my last winter with them. I want to see how they do.'
three hives in a row, each shot held still; she looks off toward the next hive, and the next shot has it in the center where our eye already rests
she lifts lids, puts an ear to the wood, writes in a notebook; minutes pass with no question pulling us on
the small surprise that ends the lull: one bee walks out onto the frosty landing board and sits in the sun

beats.note: she laughs at the bee, and says to the camera 'Tougher than me, that one,' and her voice catches

beats.note: she walks back across the white field toward the house; the camera stays with the hives as the frost begins to melt
